subtopicTitle: Thermodynamic processes — isothermal (T const), isochoric (V const), isobaric (P const), adiabatic (Q=0)

cards.front: For an ideal gas undergoing an isothermal process, what remains constant, and what is the consequence for its internal energy?
cards.back: Temperature ($T$) remains constant. For an ideal gas, internal energy ($U$) is a function of temperature only, so $\Delta U = 0$.

cards.front: What defines an isochoric process, and what is the work done by the system during such a process?
cards.back: Volume ($V$) remains constant. Since work done $W = \int P dV$, if $dV=0$, then $W = 0$.

cards.front: Derive the formula for the work done by $n$ moles of an ideal gas during a reversible isothermal expansion from $V_1$ to $V_2$.
cards.back: $W = \int_{V_1}^{V_2} P dV$. For an ideal gas, $P = \frac{nRT}{V}$. Since $T$ is constant: $$W = \int_{V_1}^{V_2} \frac{nRT}{V} dV = nRT \int_{V_1}^{V_2} \frac{1}{V} dV = nRT [\ln V]_{V_1}^{V_2} = nRT \ln\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right)$$

cards.front: What defines an adiabatic process, and how does the First Law of Thermodynamics simplify for it?
cards.back: No heat is exchanged with the surroundings, i.e., $Q=0$. The First Law of Thermodynamics states $\Delta U = Q - W$. With $Q=0$, it simplifies to $\Delta U = -W$.

cards.front: State the key relationship between pressure ($P$) and volume ($V$) for an ideal gas undergoing a reversible adiabatic process, defining any new symbols.
cards.back: $PV^\gamma = \text{constant}$, where $\gamma = C_P/C_V$ is the adiabatic index (or heat capacity ratio). $C_P$ and $C_V$ are the molar specific heats at constant pressure and volume, respectively.

cards.front: On a P-V diagram, explain why an adiabatic curve is steeper than an isothermal curve passing through the same point.
cards.back: For isothermal: $PV = \text{const} \implies P = \frac{\text{const}}{V} \implies \frac{dP}{dV} = -\frac{\text{const}}{V^2} = -\frac{P}{V}$. For adiabatic: $PV^\gamma = \text{const} \implies P = \frac{\text{const}}{V^\gamma} \implies \frac{dP}{dV} = -\gamma \frac{\text{const}}{V^{\gamma+1}} = -\gamma \frac{P}{V}$. Since $\gamma > 1$ (e.g., 1.4 for diatomic gases), the magnitude of the slope for adiabatic ($|-\gamma P/V|$) is greater than for isothermal ($|-P/V|$), making it steeper.

cards.front: For an ideal gas, summarize the First Law of Thermodynamics ($\Delta U = Q - W$) for each of the four processes: isothermal, isochoric, isobaric, and adiabatic.
cards.back:
• Isothermal ($T$ const): $\Delta U = 0 \implies Q = W$
  • Isochoric ($V$ const): $W = 0 \implies \Delta U = Q$
  • Isobaric ($P$ const): $W = P\Delta V \implies Q = \Delta U + P\Delta V$
  • Adiabatic ($Q=0$): $\Delta U = -W$
